object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier or service provider from which the organization can procure goods or services. Vendors are created during onboarding and tracked throughout their lifecycle.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master.
Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: A unique identifier generated automatically for each vendor record at creation time.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
It's the primary key. It's been the primary key since before I got here.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The official legal name of the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong. Status. Tier. The contact.

object_types.name: TaxId
object_types.definition: The tax identification number for a vendor. Not guaranteed to be unique due to organizational structures and system issues.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID.
We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The lifecycle status of a vendor record. Every vendor must be in exactly one status at any time.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended.
Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.
It defaults to draft the moment the record is created.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: A categorization of vendors based on spending volume and strategic importance. Bronze, silver, and gold represent increasing spend levels and procurement investment.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.
Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: A categorization of vendors based on risk assessment. Low, medium, high represent increasing levels of risk based on compliance review.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A formal compliance assessment of a vendor's risk profile. Each review is a timestamped record with approval signoff; vendors accumulate multiple reviews over their lifecycle, but only one is active at any time.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review. Not zero, and the one has to be signed off.
The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: ReviewId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a risk review record.

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: Region
object_types.definition: A geographic operational region. The organization uses regional sourcing models where vendors can have different contacts per region.

source_references.excerpt: Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region. So a vendor operating in EMEA and APAC has two primary contacts, one for each region.
Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

object_types.name: RegionCode
object_types.definition: The code identifying a geographic region.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

object_types.name: Contact
object_types.definition: A primary contact person for a vendor in a specific region. Multiple contacts can represent the same vendor if they operate in multiple regions.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.
Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region.
A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact. You cannot have two people both flagged primary for the same vendor in the same region -- the system rejects the second one.

ambiguities.description: Contact optionality in regions: The transcript states that a vendor operating in a region must have exactly one primary contact, but it is unclear whether every vendor must operate in at least one region, or whether a vendor can exist without any regional contacts. The statement 'If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all' suggests vendors may not operate in all regions, but does not clarify if a vendor must operate in at least one.

source_references.excerpt: Can a vendor have no contact in a region? If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Vendor status to purchase order relationship: The transcript discusses what happens to purchase orders when a vendor is suspended, but states this is an open policy question going to the steering group. Current enforcement is that you cannot create a PO against a suspended vendor at creation time, but the handling of in-flight orders (created while the vendor was active and the vendor is later suspended) is undecided. This needs explicit business rule clarification.

source_references.excerpt: Purchase orders. A PO is raised against exactly one vendor, and you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active.

If we suspend a vendor -- their review lapses, or there's a breach, or they turn up on a sanctions list -- what happens to the purchase orders already in flight? My position is that everything halts immediately. That's what suspension means.

what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided. Today's model captures three statuses and the creation-time control, and nothing about post-suspension fulfilment, because there is nothing agreed to capture.

ambiguities.description: Risk review currency: The transcript clarifies that at most one review is 'current' and a vendor's active status requires a current signed-off review. However, it is unclear how 'current' is determined (e.g., the most recent? explicitly flagged?), whether it is mutually exclusive (only one review can be current), and whether re-review cycles change which review is current. The model needed to capture 'RiskReview is_current' or similar to represent this state if it is data to be stored.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one. But one of them is the current signed-off one.
A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.

ambiguities.description: Spend tier vs. risk tier naming collision: Although the transcript clarifies that spend tier (bronze/silver/gold) and risk tier (low/medium/high) are two independent fields set by different teams, the term 'tier' is used for both in the system and in common speech. The transcript describes this as causing 'genuine chaos' but also notes that attempts to enforce 'spend tier' and 'risk tier' terminology have failed ('It's been a losing battle for two years'). For the purposes of this model, they are captured as separate object types (SpendTier, RiskTier), but stakeholders may continue to use ambiguous language.

source_references.excerpt: Tell me about tier... That's not the tier I use. I use low, medium, high... And you both call it 'tier'... Someone says 'that's a high tier vendor' in a meeting and half the room hears 'big spender' and the other half hears 'dangerous,'... Two separate fields, different values, different owners. Procurement sets one, compliance sets the other.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID uniqueness violation: The transcript explicitly states that vendors can have duplicate tax IDs ('We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident'). This is treated as a data quality problem rather than a modeling rule, but means tax ID cannot serve as a natural identifier. No constraint on TaxId uniqueness is applied to the model, but this is a known inconsistency with real-world data.

source_references.excerpt: Could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead? You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

ambiguities.description: Vendor addresses: The transcript mentions that vendors have three types of addresses (remit-to, ship-from, legal) which are 'frequently different and frequently wrong,' but these are not modeled in detail. It is unclear whether all three are mandatory, optional, or conditionally required, and whether they are captured as structured data or free text. This was noted as part of vendor record content but deferred as out of scope for today's detailed modeling.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Purchase order status and lifecycle: The transcript discusses PO number, amount, and raised date, but defers all other PO details (line items, delivery dates, cost centre, approvals, status lifecycle) as out of scope for this session. It is unclear whether a PO has a status field, what happens to its status when the vendor is suspended, or whether PO lifecycle events need to be tracked.

source_references.excerpt: There's a lot -- line items, delivery dates, cost centre, approvals. But if we go there we'll be here all day and I don't think that's what you're after today. I'll take vendor, number, amount, date and we can extend later.

ambiguities.description: PO creation control vs. Vendor active status: The transcript states you cannot create a PO against an inactive vendor ('you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active' and 'You can't create one without picking a vendor'). However, it is unclear whether the system enforces this at the database level (a foreign key constraint on an active status), or whether it is a UI/application control. The model assumes this is an integrity rule, but the implementation mechanism is not discussed.

source_references.excerpt: A PO is raised against exactly one vendor, and you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active.
You can't create one without picking a vendor. The form won't let you.

ambiguities.description: Mandatory participation in ternary contact fact: The fact type 'Vendor is_contacted_in Region by Contact' has a ternary structure. It is unclear whether a Vendor must have contacts in at least one Region (is regional coverage mandatory?), or whether a Region must always have at least one Vendor operating in it (supply presence requirement). The transcript suggests this depends on business operations, but no universal rule is stated.

source_references.excerpt: Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region. So a vendor operating in EMEA and APAC has two primary contacts, one for each region... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Preferred vendor tracking: Mei maintains a 'preferred' column in a spreadsheet outside the official system. This indicates that when multiple vendors can supply the same thing, one is designated as preferred. However, the transcript explicitly states this is ad hoc, with no defined criteria or process ('Officially nobody. In practice, me and whoever's shouting loudest that week'), and the Facilitator decides not to model it as a rule. This means the model does not capture vendor preference, competitive alternatives, or product-to-vendor mappings, even though they are business realities.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called 'preferred.' It means if two vendors can supply the same thing, buy from this one. It's not in the system anywhere. It's just my column... I'm going to note that as a gap rather than a rule, because it doesn't sound like there's a defined rule to capture yet... It's ad hoc. Don't model it.
